title: Astronomers Discover Two 'Super-Puff' Planets Lighter Than Cotton Candy
summary: Astronomers have discovered a pair of Jupiter-sized planets that are less dense than cotton candy. Named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, they orbit a Sun-like star about 1,113 light-years from Earth. These planets belong to a rare class called "super-puffs." "Only a handful of these super-puffy planets are known, and it is even rarer to find two in the same system," said Dr. George Dransfield, who led the study. The first clues came from volunteers studying data from NASA's TESS space telescope. They noticed tiny dips in the star's brightness, suggesting planets were passing in front of it. To confirm, Dr. Dransfield's team used telescopes worldwide, including the ASTEP observatory in Antarctica. Its location allowed continuous observation during the Antarctic winter, recording several complete transits. Each transit lasted over 11 hours — the longest ever observed from the ground. By measuring the star's light changes, the team determined the planets' sizes. They calculated masses by analyzing how the planets' gravity affected each other's orbits. Together, these measurements revealed extremely low densities. The two super-puffs orbit in a repeating pattern: for every five orbits of the inner planet, the outer completes three. This suggests they formed together from the same disk of gas and dust. The findings were published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on June 25, 2026. Scientists are still unsure how super-puffs form. One leading theory is that they have large amounts of hydrogen and helium gas around small solid cores. These thick atmospheres make the planets appear much larger while keeping density extremely low. Dr. Dransfield's team hopes to study their atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope to solve the mystery. This discovery gives astronomers a rare chance to study two super-puffs at once, and it may help explain how such strange, fluffy worlds form.
why_it_matters: Super-puffs sit right at the edge of what models of planet formation can explain, so finding two in one system gives astronomers a rare natural experiment: two similar worlds, same star, same origin. Solving how such fluffy planets form would sharpen our picture of how the thousands of known worlds — and maybe habitable ones — came to be.

background_read: Astronomers spot planets by watching for 'transits' — moments when a planet crosses in front of its star and makes the starlight dim slightly. NASA's TESS space telescope (the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018) was built to scan bright nearby stars for exactly those dips, and its data is public, so volunteers and students can help hunt through it.

Super-puffs are a rare family of planets, first noticed in data from NASA's Kepler space telescope (the mission that showed our galaxy is full of planets). A light-year is the distance light travels in a year — about 9.5 trillion kilometres — so a star 1,113 light-years away is far beyond anything humans could visit.

Astronomers suspect these strange worlds have small rocky cores wrapped in huge hydrogen-helium atmospheres. The James Webb Space Telescope (the largest telescope ever sent into space, launched in 2021) can split the light of a planet's atmosphere into a spectrum, which is how the team hopes to test that idea.

perspectives.description: Volunteers who sorted through telescope data get credit for spotting the first hints of real planets, and finding two super-puffs in one system is a rare chance to compare similar worlds side by side. The team also has a clear next step: reading the planets' atmospheres with the James Webb Space Telescope.

Super-puffs are so extreme that some scientists question whether their masses are measured correctly, since the gravity-based method depends on very small orbital effects. Others point out that watching 11-hour transits from the ground is slow and expensive for worlds we may never fully explain.

Super-puffs appeared in Kepler data as a small, puzzling group that models of planet formation struggle to reproduce. A 5-to-3 orbital rhythm is a classic signature of two planets that grew together in the same disk of gas and dust, so this pair works like a laboratory for testing those models.

If JWST detects hydrogen and helium escaping from these thick atmospheres, it could reveal whether super-puffs are gas giants whose outer layers are being stripped away. Every new super-puff adds a data point to a class that is still only a handful of planets strong.
